input:
When a pump draws water from an open tank, one of the most practically significant questions that arises is whether the liquid will reach the pump inlet without cavitating, and it is precisely this question that the concept of available net positive suction head is designed to answer. In the present case, the atmospheric pressure acting on the surface of the tank is 101.3 kPa, while the vapour pressure of the water at the pumping temperature is 7.4 kPa. The static lift that the liquid has to make is 2.5 m, and the friction loss in the suction line amounts to 1.2 m. In broad terms, the pressure difference between the atmosphere and the vapour pressure is what pushes the liquid towards the pump, while the lift and the friction loss work in the opposite direction, and the balance of these effects is what the calculation captures. Bringing these quantities together, the available net positive suction head, $NPSH_a$, can be expressed in terms of the atmospheric pressure, $P_{atm}$, the vapour pressure, $P_v$, the density, $\rho$, the acceleration due to gravity, $g$, the static lift, $h_{lift}$, and the friction loss, $h_f$, as follows:
$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$
Working through this relationship with the values given above leads to an available net positive suction head of 5.9 m. It should, however, be borne in mind that this available figure is only one half of the story, because the pump's required net positive suction head at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve, and the available value must exceed the required value with margin before the installation can be regarded as satisfactory from a cavitation standpoint.

Available net positive suction head, $NPSH_a$, is calculated from the pressure at the surface of an open tank, the vapour pressure of the water at the pumping temperature, the static lift, and the friction loss in the suction line. The tank is open, so the surface pressure is the atmospheric pressure. The atmospheric pressure is 101.3 kPa and the vapour pressure is 7.4 kPa; the static lift, $h_{lift}$, is 2.5 m and the suction-line friction loss, $h_f$, is 1.2 m. For water of density $\rho$ under gravity $g$, the relation is
$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$
where $P_{atm}$ denotes the atmospheric pressure and $P_v$ denotes the vapour pressure. Substitution of the stated values gives an available net positive suction head of 5.9 m. The pressure term is the head that the atmosphere can support above the vapour pressure of the liquid at its pumping temperature. Each term in the relation is a head in metres, so the terms can be added and subtracted directly. Static lift and friction loss consume part of that head before the liquid reaches the pump inlet, and the remainder is the head available against cavitation at the duty flow. The pump's required net positive suction head at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve, and the available value must exceed the required value with margin. The comparison is therefore between a calculated available head and a vendor figure for the actual machine, and the brief states no numerical margin. A margin stated without the vendor value would be unsupported, so the worked result closes at the available head and the condition it must satisfy.
